why: Gathering requirements and writing clear user stories is the core of a Business Analyst job. Case-study interviews ask you to do exactly this live.
outcome: run a discovery interview, write user stories with testable acceptance criteria, map gaps and prepare a UAT.

lessons.title: Discover the real need
text: People ask for solutions ('add an Excel export'); your job is to find the problem behind it ('the manager needs a weekly view of late orders'). Ask why, ask for examples, ask what happens today.
Identify stakeholders early: who uses it, who pays, who decides, who is impacted. Their goals often conflict.
points: Open questions: 'Walk me through the last time you did this'.
Capture current state (as-is) before designing the target (to-be).
Note business rules, exceptions and volumes: 'what if the client has two addresses?'.
Prioritise with MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).
Summarise and validate in writing after each workshop.

lessons.title: User stories and acceptance criteria
text: A user story describes a need from the user's point of view: As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>. It is a placeholder for a conversation, not a full specification.
Acceptance criteria make the story testable. Given / When / Then (Gherkin) describes each scenario precisely.
points: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Split big stories by workflow step, business rule or data variation, not by technical layer.
Cover the happy path, the errors and the edge cases in the criteria.
Attach mock-ups or examples when the UI matters.

example.code:
Story: As a job seeker, I want to filter offers by minimum salary,
       so that I only see offers I would accept.

Scenario: Offers below the minimum are hidden
  Given offers with salaries 35k, 45k and 60k
  When I set the minimum salary to 40k
  Then I see the 45k and 60k offers only

Scenario: Offers without a salary
  Given an offer with no salary information
  When I set a minimum salary
  Then the offer is shown with the label "Salary not specified"

lessons.title: Gap analysis and UAT
text: Gap analysis compares the current state with the target and lists what must change: process, data, tools, people. It turns a vision into a backlog.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT, 'recette' in French) is when business users confirm the solution meets their needs before go-live. The BA usually prepares and runs it.
points: Gap table columns: area, as-is, to-be, gap, action, owner, priority.
UAT test cases come from the acceptance criteria.
Each test case: preconditions, steps, expected result, actual result, status.
Log defects with steps to reproduce, severity and screenshots; agree go / no-go criteria up front.

lessons.title: Prioritise, trace and manage change
text: There is never time for everything. MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must, Should, Could and Won't (this time) with the stakeholders, so the release is defined by its Musts. Value versus effort and the cost of delay help break ties between Shoulds.

A traceability matrix links each requirement to its source, its user stories and its test cases: you can prove every Must is tested and see what a change affects. Changes will come; handle them with a light change process: describe it, assess the impact on scope, time and cost, decide with the sponsor, and update the backlog and the matrix.
points: If everything is a Must, nothing is: aim for about 60% of the effort on Musts.
Write down what is out of scope; it prevents most disputes.
Every change request gets an impact assessment before a yes.
Keep one source of truth (the backlog tool) rather than requirements scattered in emails.

example.code:
ID    Requirement                     Priority  Source          Story    Test case   Status
R-12  Export the claims list to CSV   Must      Claims manager  CL-88    TC-201/202  Done
R-13  Filter claims by status         Should    Workshop 03/10  CL-91    TC-210      In UAT
R-14  Email a weekly summary          Could     Director        -        -           Backlog
R-15  Mobile app                      Won't     -               -        -           Out of scope (v2)
example.note: One line per requirement: where it came from, how it is built and how it is tested.

lessons.title: Elicitation techniques and running a workshop
text: No single technique finds every requirement. Interviews give depth and the political picture, but people describe what they think they do. Observation (job shadowing) shows the real work: the workarounds, the Excel file kept on the side, the sticky notes on the screen. Document analysis (procedures, existing reports, screens, tickets, regulations) gives you the rules and the vocabulary before you meet anyone, so you ask better questions. Surveys reach many users but mostly confirm hypotheses you already have. Combine them: read first, interview, observe, then converge in a workshop.

A good interview is prepared: a goal, eight to ten open questions, and requests for the last real case rather than the general rule ('show me the last claim you rejected'). Leave silence after a question; the useful detail often comes second. End with 'who else should I talk to?' and 'what did I not ask?'. Send a short written summary within a day: the corrections people make to it are often worth more than the interview itself.

A workshop brings several stakeholders together to decide or converge, which a series of interviews cannot do. It needs a precise objective ('agree on the claim approval rules'), the right five to eight people including someone who can decide, a timeboxed agenda, a facilitator who is not also the main contributor, and a visible artefact everyone works on: a process on the wall, a list of rules, a prototype. Keep a 'parking lot' for off-topic points so they are noted without derailing the session. Close with the decisions taken, the open questions with an owner and a date, and the next steps.
points: Read the documents before the first meeting: you arrive with the vocabulary and precise questions.
Ask 'show me' as often as 'tell me': observation reveals workarounds nobody mentions.
Separate the facilitator and note-taker roles whenever you can.
Write decisions and open questions on a shared screen during the workshop, not afterwards.
Prototypes and real examples trigger more precise feedback than abstract questions.

example.code:
# Workshop: claim approval rules (2h, on site)
Objective: agree on who approves a claim and above which amount
Participants: claims manager (decides), 2 handlers, finance controller, IT lead, BA (facilitator), PO (notes)
Pre-read: current procedure v3, 10 real claims from last month

| Time | Topic                                 | Output                     |
|------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| 0:00 | Goal, scope, rules of the session     | Shared objective           |
| 0:10 | Walk through 3 real claims            | Steps and exceptions noted |
| 0:50 | Draft approval rules on the board     | Rule list v1               |
| 1:30 | Check the rules against the 10 claims | Rules confirmed or changed |
| 1:50 | Decisions, open questions, next steps | Owners and dates           |

Parking lot: notification emails, archive period
example.note: Real cases as pre-read and as test material keep the discussion concrete.

lessons.title: Testable acceptance criteria and non-functional requirements
text: A criterion is testable when two people running it would agree on pass or fail. 'Easy to use', 'fast' and 'secure' are not testable; 'the search returns results in under 2 seconds for 95% of requests' is. Write criteria from the user's observable behaviour rather than the implementation, and use concrete data. Gherkin gives the structure: Given (the context), When (one action), Then (the observable outcome). A Scenario Outline with an Examples table covers a business rule with several values without copying the scenario.

Business rules need explicit boundaries. If free shipping applies 'above 100 euros', is exactly 100 included? Boundary values are where many defects hide, so put them in the examples. Keep one behaviour per scenario, and avoid steps such as 'click the blue button' unless the interface itself is what you are specifying: they break with every redesign and hide the rule.

Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well the system works: performance, availability, security, accessibility, usability, compliance (GDPR, retention periods), scalability, maintainability. They are often forgotten because nobody asks for them until production fails. Make each one measurable with a metric, a target and a context, and decide where it lives: in the Definition of Done when it applies to every story (accessibility checks, security review), or as acceptance criteria on the story it concerns.
points: Testable means observable, measurable, with concrete data and a clear pass or fail.
Use Scenario Outline and Examples for rules with several values, including the boundaries.
Ask NFR questions during discovery: how many users, how fast, kept how long, who may see what.
'Highly available' is a wish; '99.5% per month during office hours' is a requirement.
Review NFRs with the tech lead or architect: some are expensive and change the design.

example.code:
Feature: Shipping fee

  Scenario Outline: Free shipping from 100 euros
    Given a basket total of <total> euros
    When I go to checkout
    Then the shipping fee is <fee> euros

    Examples:
      | total  | fee  |
      | 99.99  | 4.90 |
      | 100.00 | 0.00 |
      | 150.00 | 0.00 |
example.note: The boundary (exactly 100) is written down, so nobody has to guess whether it is included.

lessons.title: Prioritisation beyond MoSCoW: cost of delay, WSJF and Kano
text: MoSCoW defines a release scope, but it says little about the order inside the Musts, and stakeholders tend to call everything a Must. Value versus effort is a quick next step: place items on a two-by-two grid; high value and low effort items (quick wins) go first, low value and high effort items are questioned. The scores are relative estimates, so agree on them together rather than letting each requester score their own item.

Cost of delay asks what we lose for each week an item is not delivered: revenue, a regulatory penalty, a missed market window, a growing risk. WSJF (Weighted Shortest Job First), popularised by SAFe, divides the cost of delay by the job size. The cost of delay is the sum of three relative scores: business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement, usually on a Fibonacci-like scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20). The highest WSJF goes first, so small items with a high cost of delay rise to the top.

The Kano model classifies features by their effect on satisfaction. Basic needs cause anger when missing but no delight when present: the login works, the invoice is correct. Performance needs increase satisfaction in proportion: faster search, more filters. Delighters surprise and please but nobody expects them, and over time they become basic needs. Kano reminds you to secure the basics first, then compete on performance, and keep room for a few delighters. Whatever the method, the output is a ranked list with its rationale, shared with the sponsor.
points: Score each item relative to the others, not in absolute terms.
WSJF favours small, urgent items; split big items so their value is not hidden in a large size.
A regulatory deadline has a high time criticality: missing it has a fixed, known cost.
A Kano survey asks two questions per feature: how would you feel if it is present, and if it is absent?
Record the decision and its reasons next to the ranking so it is not renegotiated every week.

example.code:
Item                          Value  Time crit.  Risk/Opp.  CoD  Size  WSJF
GDPR data export (deadline)     5       13          8       26    5    5.2
Claim status in client app      8        3          3       14    3    4.7
Bulk upload of claims           5        5          5       15    8    1.9
New dashboard for directors    13        2          1       16   13    1.2

Order: GDPR export, client status, bulk upload, dashboard
example.note: CoD = value + time criticality + risk/opportunity; WSJF = CoD / size. The big dashboard drops despite its high value.

lessons.title: Data requirements and documentation that stays usable
text: Many projects are really about data: a report, an interface, a migration, a dashboard. 'Show the customers' is not a requirement until you know which customers, which fields, from which source, how fresh and with which rules. A data dictionary lists each business data element with its definition, type and format, allowed values, source system, owner, whether it is mandatory and whether it is sensitive (personal data). It ends arguments such as 'active customer' meaning three different things in three departments.

A report specification describes the purpose and audience, the questions the report answers, each measure with its exact calculation rule, the dimensions and filters, the level of detail, the refresh frequency, the data sources, who may see what, and a mock-up. For each measure, write a worked example with real numbers that the business validates: it becomes the test case. Ask about history ('do we change last month's figures when a claim is reopened?') and about missing or late data.

Documentation only helps if people find it and trust it. In Confluence, keep one page per topic with an owner and a status (draft, validated), a decision log, and links to the Jira epics instead of copied text. In Jira, use the hierarchy (epic, story, sub-task) consistently, one need per story, the acceptance criteria in the ticket itself, labels and components agreed with the team, and close what is obsolete. A backlog of 600 tickets that nobody reads is not a source of truth.
points: Define every business term once in the glossary or data dictionary and link to it.
Each measure gets a formula, a worked example and an owner who validates it.
Flag personal and sensitive data early: it drives access rights and GDPR retention.
Link Confluence pages and Jira tickets rather than duplicating content.
Archive stale pages and close stale tickets: an outdated document is worse than none.

example.code:
| Field           | Definition                                 | Type / format     | Allowed values                  | Source    | Mandatory | Sensitive  |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|---------------------------------|-----------|-----------|------------|
| claim_id        | Unique claim reference                     | Text, CL-000000   | -                               | ClaimsApp | Yes       | No         |
| claim_status    | Current step of the claim                  | Code              | OPEN, IN_REVIEW, PAID, REJECTED | ClaimsApp | Yes       | No         |
| claim_amount    | Amount claimed, VAT included               | Decimal(10,2) EUR | >= 0                            | ClaimsApp | Yes       | No         |
| customer_email  | Contact email of the policyholder          | Text, email       | -                               | CRM       | No        | Yes (GDPR) |
| active_customer | Has at least one policy in force today     | Boolean           | true / false                    | Derived   | Yes       | No         |
example.note: Extract of a data dictionary: one line per business field, agreed with the data owners.

lessons.title: Test plan, test cases and defect triage (UAT / recette)
text: UAT is the last check before go-live, so it needs a plan, not a list of things to click. A test strategy says what is tested, at which level and by whom: the supplier or the IT team runs the unit, integration and system tests (in France often called 'recette usine' or 'recette technique'), and the business users run the acceptance tests ('recette fonctionnelle' or 'recette utilisateur'). The test plan for a campaign then fixes the scope (which stories and processes), the dates, the environment, the test data, the testers and their availability, the tools, and two sets of criteria agreed with the sponsor up front: entry criteria (the build is installed, the data is loaded, the testers are trained) and exit criteria (what must be true to say go).

Test cases are written from the acceptance criteria, before the build arrives. Each one has an identifier, the story or requirement it covers, a precondition, the steps, the test data and the expected result; the tester then records the actual result and a status (passed, failed, blocked, not run). Cover the normal case, then each rule, the boundary values (49,999.99, 50,000.00 and 50,000.01 when the limit is 50,000) and the error cases, with realistic data that respects GDPR: anonymised or invented customers, never a copy of real records shared by email. In France the set of test cases for a campaign is often called the 'cahier de recette'. The traceability matrix then shows that every Must requirement has at least one test case, and after the run, which ones passed.

A UAT campaign is run with the business, not for it. Pick testers who know the real work, block their time with their managers, give them a short briefing and a test environment that looks like production. Hold a short daily meeting during the campaign: test cases run and passed, new defects, blocking points. Testers should also try their real daily cases outside the script (exploratory testing): it is often where the missing rule appears. The BA prepares the cases, helps the testers, checks each defect report and keeps the figures up to date.

Every failed check becomes a defect ('anomalie') with a title, the steps to reproduce, the data used, the expected and actual results, a screenshot, the environment and the version. Severity is the impact on the business or the system; priority is how urgently it must be fixed, decided in triage with the product owner. French teams usually grade severity as 'bloquante' (blocking: a main process cannot be done and there is no workaround), 'majeure' (major: a function is wrong but a workaround exists) and 'mineure' (minor: cosmetic or low impact). The two differ: a typo in the company name on the login page is minor but high priority; a wrong total in a yearly report used in December may be major but less urgent in March. A defect goes through a life cycle: new, triaged (or rejected as not a defect, or marked duplicate), assigned, fixed, ready for retest, then closed when the tester confirms the fix, or reopened. Each fix also needs a short regression test on the nearby functions.

At the end of the campaign, the go / no-go meeting compares the figures with the exit criteria: share of test cases run and passed, open defects by severity, workarounds and fix dates for what remains. The decision belongs to the sponsor or the business owner, not to the BA. The result is written in the 'PV de recette' (procès-verbal de recette, the acceptance report), signed by the business owner: acceptance without reservations, acceptance with reservations (the open defects listed, each with an owner and a fix date), or refusal. Tools: Jira with Xray or Zephyr for test cases linked to stories, Squash TM (open source, widely used in France), or a shared spreadsheet for a small campaign, as long as the traceability is kept.
points: Agree on entry and exit criteria with the sponsor before the campaign starts, not during the go / no-go meeting.
One test case checks one thing: precondition, steps, data, expected result.
Test the boundaries and the error cases, not only the normal path.
Severity is the impact, priority is the urgency: grade them separately.
A fixed defect is closed only after a retest by the business, plus a regression check around it.

example.code:
Test plan  UAT claims app v2      Campaign 02-13 March   Testers: 6 claims handlers
Entry: build 2.4 on the UAT environment, test data loaded, testers trained
Exit:  100% of Must test cases run, 0 blocking and at most 2 major defects open (workaround + fix date)

ID      Story   Precondition                Steps / data                             Expected result
TC-301  CL-120  Policy P-1001 in force      Submit claim, water damage, 1,200 EUR    Reference CL-xxxxxx shown, status OPEN
TC-302  CL-120  Policy P-1001 in force      Submit claim dated tomorrow              Error: incident date in the future
TC-303  CL-120  Policy P-1001 in force      Submit claim of 50,000.01 EUR            Message: call your advisor, no claim created
TC-304  CL-121  Policy P-2002 cancelled     Submit claim, theft, 300 EUR             Error: no policy in force on that date

Defect D-17  TC-303  Severity: major  Priority: high  Status: Fixed -> Ready for retest
Steps: policy P-1001, amount 50,000.01, Submit  |  Actual: claim CL-004512 created  |  Screenshot attached
example.note: Extract of a test plan, its test cases and one defect: each case traces to a story, each defect to a case.

lessons.title: Writing a functional specification (SFD)
text: In French projects you will meet three documents that are often confused. The 'cahier des charges' (fonctionnel) is written by the client side, the business owner ('maîtrise d'ouvrage', MOA): it describes the context, the goals, the expected functions at a high level and the constraints (budget, deadline, standards), often to choose a supplier in a call for tenders. The SFD ('spécifications fonctionnelles détaillées', detailed functional specification) describes precisely how the solution must behave, screen by screen and rule by rule; it is written by the BA, on the client or the supplier side ('maîtrise d'oeuvre', MOE), sometimes after more general specifications (SFG). User stories slice the same need into small backlog items with acceptance criteria. The technical design (STD, 'spécifications techniques détaillées') belongs to the development team.

A useful SFD follows a stable structure: the context and goals, the scope (in and out), the actors and their roles, the processes or use cases with their main and alternative flows, the screens with every field (format, mandatory or not, default value, checks), the business rules, the error cases and their messages, the data (with links to the data dictionary), the interfaces with other systems, the non-functional requirements, and the open questions. Give every rule and every message an identifier (RG-07, E-03) so that test cases, defects and discussions point to it instead of quoting a paragraph.

Write rules that can be tested. 'Large claims are checked' is not a rule; 'A claim above 50,000.00 EUR cannot be submitted online; the advisor's phone number is shown' is. Name the actor, the condition, the exact threshold with its unit, whether the limit is included, and the result, and add a worked example with figures that the business validates. One rule per line, no 'etc.', no 'if possible', and the same term everywhere: if the glossary says 'policyholder', do not switch to 'client' two pages later. A rule written this way gives you its test cases almost for free: one at the threshold, one just above, one just below.

An SFD is a living document under change control. Keep a version number, a change log saying what changed, why and on whose decision, and a status: draft, under review, validated. Sign-off ('validation') by the business owner turns it into the reference for development, testing and acceptance; after that, every change goes through the change process, with its impact on cost, dates and tests. Store it where the team works (Confluence, SharePoint) and link it to the Jira epics rather than copying text into every ticket, so there is one source of truth.

Agile teams do not write a 300-page SFD before starting, but many still need specifications. Teams write them when the rules are complex or regulated (insurance, banking, payroll, healthcare), when a supplier builds the solution under a fixed-price contract, when an interface must be agreed with another team or company, or when auditors and the support team need a reference after go-live. The common compromise is a light, living specification per epic or feature (rules, screens, data, error cases) next to the stories, which keep the acceptance criteria for each slice. In interviews, show that you choose the level of detail according to the risk and the audience, not out of habit.
points: Cahier des charges = the need (client side); SFD = how the solution behaves, in detail; user story = one slice of value in the backlog.
Give every business rule and error message an identifier and trace it to its test cases.
A testable rule names the actor, the condition, the exact threshold and unit, and the result.
Version, change log, status and a named business sign-off: without them, nobody knows which version is the reference.
In agile teams, keep a light, living specification per feature for complex or regulated rules, linked to the stories.

example.code:
SFD  Claims app v2  Section 4.2: Submit a claim online       Version 1.3, validated 12/02 (claims manager)

Actor: policyholder signed in            Trigger: "Declare a claim" button
Fields: incident date (mandatory, date), type (list: water, theft, glass, fire), amount (mandatory, EUR, 2 decimals),
        description (optional, 1,000 characters), photos (optional, JPG / PNG / PDF, 10 MB each)

RG-07  The incident date is on or before today and on or after the policy start date.
RG-08  An amount above 50,000.00 EUR is not submitted online: the advisor's phone number is shown.
RG-09  A glass claim under 300.00 EUR is approved automatically (status PAID within 2 working days).

E-03   "The incident date cannot be in the future."            (RG-07)
E-04   "Please call your advisor for claims above 50,000 EUR."  (RG-08)

Change log: 1.2 -> 1.3  RG-09 threshold 250 -> 300 EUR (decision of 10/02, claims committee)
example.note: Extract of an SFD section: actor, fields, numbered rules and messages, and the change log.

items: Get from requested solution to real need
As a ..., I want ..., so that ...
Story is clear enough to start
Watch the real work, find the workarounds
Rules and vocabulary from existing material
One Gherkin scenario, several data rows
How well: performance, security, availability, compliance
What we lose per week of waiting
Definition, format, source, owner per field
Measures with rules, filters, refresh, access
The set of test cases for a UAT campaign
When the campaign can start / what must be true to say go
Impact on the business vs urgency of the fix
Signed acceptance report: accepted, with reservations, or refused
Detailed functional specification: rules, screens, fields, errors

pitfalls: Writing the solution the stakeholder asked for without understanding the problem.
Stories with no acceptance criteria, or criteria that cannot be tested ('the page is fast').
Forgetting edge cases and error cases.
Starting UAT without agreed exit criteria.
Running a workshop without a clear objective or without a decision-maker in the room: a lot of discussion, no decision.
Discovering non-functional requirements at go-live ('it must handle 5,000 users') because nobody asked during discovery.
Report measures without a written calculation rule, so each team computes 'active customer' its own way.
Starting UAT with test cases that only follow the normal path: the boundary values and the error cases are where the defects are.

exercises.q: Rewrite as a user story: 'We need a CSV export button on the applications page'.
exercises.answer: As a job seeker, I want to download my applications as a file, so that I can share my progress with my career coach. (Then confirm with the user whether CSV, PDF or a share link best serves that goal.)

exercises.q: Write acceptance criteria for 'reset my password'.
exercises.answer:
Given I have an account
When I request a password reset with my email
Then I receive a reset link valid for 1 hour

Given the link has expired
When I open it
Then I see a message and can request a new link

Given I enter an unknown email
When I request a reset
Then I see the same confirmation message (no account disclosure)

exercises.q: Two stakeholders want contradictory features. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Make the conflict explicit with facts (goals, impact, cost), bring both to the decision-maker (often the Product Owner or sponsor) with options and a recommendation, and document the decision.

exercises.q: Two days before UAT, a director asks to add a new approval step to the process. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Thank them and capture the request precisely, then assess the impact with the team: process and screens to change, rules, tests, training, and the effect on the UAT date. Present the options to the sponsor: include it and move the date, deliver it in the next release, or swap it with a lower-priority item. Once decided, update the backlog, the traceability matrix and the test plan, and tell everyone affected.

exercises.q: You join a project to replace the tool used by 40 claims handlers. Which elicitation techniques do you use, and in which order?
exercises.answer: First document analysis: the current procedure, screens, reports, a sample of real claims and recent incidents, to learn the vocabulary and prepare questions. Then interviews with the claims manager, a few handlers of different seniority, finance and IT. Then observation of two or three handlers for half a day to see the real work and the workarounds. Finally workshops to agree on the target process and rules with a decision-maker in the room, and a quick prototype to collect feedback.

exercises.q: Make this requirement testable: 'The search must be fast and the customer data must be secure.'
exercises.answer: Split it into measurable criteria, for example: the search returns results in under 2 seconds for 95% of requests with 50,000 offers and 200 concurrent users; only users with the 'advisor' role can see the customer's phone and email; every access to a customer record is logged with user, date and record; customer data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Then confirm the targets with the business and the tech lead.

exercises.q: Rank by WSJF: A has a cost of delay of 20 and a size of 10, B a cost of delay of 9 and a size of 3, C a cost of delay of 13 and a size of 13.
exercises.answer: WSJF = cost of delay / size: A = 2, B = 3, C = 1. Order: B, then A, then C. B goes first although it has the smallest cost of delay, because it is small and delivers value quickly.

exercises.q: A director asks for 'a monthly claims report'. List the questions you ask before writing the specification.
exercises.answer: What decision will the report support and who reads it? Which measures exactly (number of claims, amounts, handling time) and with which calculation rules? Which breakdowns and filters (region, product, status)? Monthly as of which date, and are past months restated when a claim changes? Which source system, and how are missing data handled? Who may see it, at which level of detail? Format and delivery (dashboard, export, email)? Then build a mock-up with real figures and have it validated.

exercises.q: Sort these requirements: functional (what the system does) or non-functional (how well it does it).

groups.name: Functional
items: The user can export the report as CSV
The system emails a reset link when asked
An admin can deactivate an account

groups.name: Non-functional
items: 95% of pages load in under 2 seconds
The service is available 99.9% of the month
Personal data is encrypted at rest

exercises.answer: Functional requirements describe behaviour and become user stories with acceptance criteria; non-functional ones (performance, availability, security, accessibility) apply across stories and must be measurable to be tested.

exercises.q: Fill in the Gherkin keywords of this acceptance criterion.
exercises.snippet:
Feature: Password reset
  Scenario: Reset link sent to a known email
    ___ an account exists for "lea@example.com"
    ___ Lea asks for a password reset with "lea@example.com"
    ___ she receives a reset link valid for 30 minutes
exercises.answer: Given sets the context, When is the user’s action, Then is the observable result (add And for more steps). One scenario tests one behaviour; write another one for an unknown email.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Business Analyst (1/5). A chain of 13 shops wants “click & collect”. The sponsor said release 1 is only: pay online, then pick up in a shop. Sort the notes from the kick-off workshop.

groups.name: Functional (release 1)
items: Customers choose a shop and a pickup slot when paying online
Each shop gets the list of orders to prepare
Customers get a message when their order is ready

groups.name: Non-functional (release 1)
items: The pickup page loads in under 2 seconds on a phone
Order data is deleted 3 years after the pickup
The pages work with a screen reader (WCAG 2.1 AA)

groups.name: Out of scope for release 1
items: Loyalty points on click & collect orders

exercises.hint: Release 1 = pay online + pick up in a shop. A requirement about how well the system works (speed, retention, accessibility) is non-functional.
exercises.answer: Writing the scope down at the start (in and out) is what protects the deadline: delivery, loyalty and cash payment are real ideas, so record them in the backlog as later items instead of dropping them. Non-functional requirements need a number or a standard (2 seconds, 3 years, WCAG 2.1 AA), otherwise nobody can test them.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Business Analyst (2/5). Put the to-be process for one click & collect order in order, from payment to pickup.
steps: The customer pays online and picks a shop and a slot
The order reaches the shop’s preparation list
A shop employee picks the items and marks the order “ready”
The customer gets a message with a pickup code
The customer shows the code at the counter
The employee hands over the order and marks it “collected”
exercises.hint: Follow the order: online, then the shop’s back office, then the customer, then the counter.
exercises.answer: This sequence is the backbone of a BPMN diagram (one lane for the customer, one for the shop) and of the story map: each step becomes one or more user stories. The status changes (ready, collected) are what the system must record, so they are also your data requirements and the basis of the reports (orders not collected after 48 h, preparation time per shop).

exercises.q: Take-home case, Business Analyst (3/5). The sponsor wants to pilot in 3 cities. Use the order history (practice database shop): the 3 cities with the most orders, with the number of customers who ordered, the number of orders and the revenue (sum of total, rounded to 2 decimals), most orders first.
exercises.hint: Join customers and orders, GROUP BY city, COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) for customers, ORDER BY orders DESC LIMIT 3.
exercises.answer:
SELECT c.city,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS customers,
       COUNT(o.id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(o.total), 2) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY orders DESC
LIMIT 3;
exercises.explain: Paris (5 customers, 14 orders, 3,569.05), Lyon (3 customers, 9 orders, 1,361.56) and Marseille (4 customers, 6 orders, 867.08). Note what the data cannot say: Lille has fewer orders (5) but more revenue (1,331.01) than Marseille. A business analyst gives the sponsor both views and the question to decide: do we pilot where most orders are (operations test) or where the money is?

exercises.q: Take-home case, Business Analyst (4/5). Release 1 has 6 weeks. With MoSCoW, which item is a Must: without it, click & collect cannot work at all?
options: Choosing the pickup shop when paying
A text message when the order is ready (an e-mail could do it)
A map of the shops on the home page
Pickup slots of 15 minutes instead of half-days
exercises.answer: A Must is something release 1 cannot go live without: without a chosen shop, no order can be prepared or collected. The text message is a Should (an e-mail covers the need), the map and finer slots are Coulds. Write the reason next to each priority: it ends most arguments in the planning meeting.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Business Analyst (5/5). Write the user story for “the customer is told the order is ready”, with 2 or 3 acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then, and 2 questions you still need to ask the shops.
exercises.hint: As a … I want … so that …; one scenario per behaviour (ready on time, not collected, wrong shop); questions about how the shops really work.
exercises.answer:
Story: As a click & collect customer, I want to be told when my order is ready, so that I only go to the shop when I can collect it.
AC1: Given my order is marked “ready” by the shop, When the status changes, Then I receive a message within 5 minutes with the shop’s address, opening hours and my pickup code.
AC2: Given my order has been ready for 48 hours, When it is still not collected, Then I receive one reminder, and the shop sees the order in its “not collected” list.
AC3: Given the shop marks an item as missing, When the order is marked ready, Then the message lists the missing item and the refunded amount.
Questions for the shops: How long do you keep an order that is not collected, and what happens then (refund, back to stock)? Who marks orders ready at busy times, and on which device?

exercises.q: Put the steps of a UAT campaign in order.
steps: Agree on the scope, the dates and the entry and exit criteria with the sponsor
Write the test cases from the acceptance criteria and prepare the test data
Check the entry criteria: build installed, data loaded, testers trained
Run the test cases and log each defect with steps to reproduce
Triage the defects, fix them, then retest and run regression checks
Hold the go / no-go meeting and sign the acceptance report (PV de recette)
exercises.answer: The criteria come first so the go / no-go meeting compares figures with rules agreed in advance, not opinions. Test cases are written before the build arrives, from the acceptance criteria; the campaign starts only when the entry criteria are met, otherwise testers lose days on an environment that is not ready.

exercises.q: Grade each defect found during the UAT of a claims app: blocking, major or minor.

groups.name: Blocking (bloquante)
items: No claim can be submitted: the Submit button returns an error, with no other way to do it
The payment file sent to the bank doubles every amount

groups.name: Major (majeure)
items: The status filter ignores “In review”, but handlers can sort the list by status instead
The CSV export fails; the same list can be printed from the screen

groups.name: Minor (mineure)
items: A typo in the label of the Cancel button
Column widths are uneven on a small laptop screen

exercises.answer: Blocking: a main process cannot be done, or the result is wrong with serious consequences, and there is no workaround. Major: a function is wrong but a workaround exists. Minor: cosmetic or low impact. Priority is decided separately in triage: a minor typo in the company name on the login page can still be fixed first.

exercises.q: Match each test term to its definition.
pairs: Precondition, steps, data and expected result for one check
Links each requirement to its stories and test cases
The impact of a defect on the business or the system
How urgently a defect must be fixed
Re-runs existing tests to check that a fix broke nothing else
The conditions agreed in advance to say go at the end of the campaign
exercises.answer: These terms are how a BA, the testers and the delivery team talk about a campaign. Severity and priority are set separately: the tester proposes the severity, the product owner sets the priority in triage.

exercises.q: Scenario: the UAT of the claims app ends on Thursday and go-live is planned on Monday. Make each decision.

steps.text: 96% of the test cases passed, but one blocking defect is open: claims above 10,000 EUR cannot be paid.

choices.label: Go live and fix it in the first week
choices.feedback: The exit criteria say 0 blocking defects. Large claims would be stuck from day one, with angry customers and a manual backlog to clear.

choices.label: Report it to the sponsor: no-go unless the fix is delivered and retested before the decision
choices.feedback: You state the facts against the agreed criteria and leave the decision to the sponsor, with a clear condition for go.

choices.label: Downgrade it to major so the figures meet the criteria
choices.feedback: Hiding a blocking defect destroys the trust in the campaign figures, and the problem is still there on Monday.

steps.text: The fix arrives on Friday morning.

choices.label: Close the defect: the developer says it is fixed
choices.feedback: A defect is closed by a retest on the UAT environment, not by the person who fixed it.

choices.label: Retest the failed case with a business tester, plus a short regression check on payments, then update the figures
choices.feedback: The fix is confirmed where it failed, and you check it did not break the nearby payment cases.

choices.label: Rerun the whole campaign of 300 test cases
choices.feedback: Not possible before Monday and not needed: target the retest and the regression on the impacted area.

steps.text: Two major defects remain, each with a documented workaround and a fix planned in the release two weeks later. The exit criteria allow up to two.

choices.label: Go, with an acceptance report signed with reservations listing both defects, their owners and fix dates
choices.feedback: The decision matches the agreed criteria and the reservations are written down, so the fixes are tracked after go-live.

choices.label: No-go until every defect is closed
choices.feedback: Stricter than the criteria everyone agreed: a release with known, managed defects and workarounds is normal.

choices.label: Go, and mention the two defects in a chat message
choices.feedback: Nothing formal: after go-live nobody can prove what was accepted, and the fixes may be forgotten.

exercises.answer: Compare the facts with the exit criteria agreed before the campaign, let the sponsor decide, close defects only after a business retest, and write the reservations in the PV de recette.

exercises.q: In E2, count the defects that are still open (status “Open”) with severity Blocking or Major, for the go / no-go meeting.
exercises.answer: =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"Blocking",C2:C9,"Open")+COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"Major",C2:C9,"Open")
exercises.explain: 3 defects: D-05 (blocking) and D-02, D-06 (major). COUNTIFS applies all its criteria together (AND), so add two COUNTIFS for “Blocking or Major”. D-08 is waiting for a retest: it is not closed either, so mention it in the meeting, and agree in the exit criteria which statuses count as open.

exercises.q: Sort each item into the document where it belongs.

groups.name: Cahier des charges (the need)
items: The business goals, the context, the budget and the deadline
The functions expected at a high level, written by the client for a call for tenders

groups.name: SFD (detailed specification)
items: Every field of the claim screen with its format, mandatory flag and checks
The numbered business rules (RG-07, RG-08…) and their error messages

groups.name: User story (backlog item)
items: “As a policyholder, I want…, so that…” with a few acceptance criteria
A slice of value small enough to be built in one sprint

exercises.answer: The cahier des charges says what the client needs and within which constraints; the SFD describes in detail how the solution behaves; user stories slice the work for the team and carry the acceptance criteria of each slice. In agile teams the SFD is often a light page per feature, linked to the stories.

exercises.q: Write 5 test cases (ID, precondition, steps and data, expected result) for the story “Submit a claim online”, from these acceptance criteria: (1) a policyholder with a policy in force can submit a claim with an incident date, a type and an amount, and gets a reference CL-xxxxxx; (2) the incident date cannot be in the future or before the policy start date; (3) the amount must be above 0 and at most 50,000.00 EUR, above that the advisor's phone number is shown and no claim is created; (4) photos are optional, JPG, PNG or PDF, 10 MB each at most.
exercises.hint: One check per case; the normal case first, then each rule with its boundaries and an error case.
exercises.answer:
TC-01  Policy P-1001 in force since 01/01. Submit: today's date, water damage, 1,200.00 EUR, no photo. Expected: reference CL-xxxxxx shown, claim status OPEN.
TC-02  Same policy. Submit with the incident date = tomorrow. Expected: error “The incident date cannot be in the future”, no claim created.
TC-03  Policy P-3003 starting on 01/03. Submit with the incident date 28/02. Expected: error, the date is before the policy start; no claim created.
TC-04  Policy P-1001. Submit 50,000.00 EUR, then a second claim of 50,000.01 EUR. Expected: the first is accepted (limit included); the second shows the advisor's phone number and creates no claim.
TC-05  Policy P-1001. Attach a 9 MB JPG, then a 12 MB PDF, then a .docx file. Expected: the JPG is accepted; the 12 MB file and the .docx are refused with a message naming the allowed formats and size.
Also worth adding: amount 0 or negative (refused), a cancelled policy (refused), and a check that the claim appears in the handler's list. Link each case to the story in the traceability matrix.

interview.q: How do you gather requirements from a stakeholder who doesn't know what they want?
interview.a: Start from their current process and pain points, observe them working, use examples and quick mock-ups to react to, and iterate. People are better at reacting to something concrete than describing needs in the abstract.

interview.q: What makes a good user story?
interview.a: It follows INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable to a user, estimable, small enough for a sprint, and testable thanks to clear acceptance criteria.

interview.q: What is your role in UAT?
interview.a: Prepare the test plan and cases from the acceptance criteria, organise the testers and environment, follow up defects with the team, report progress and help the business make the go / no-go decision.

interview.q: How do you handle conflicting priorities between two stakeholders?
interview.a: I make the conflict explicit with facts: what each request brings, its cost and its link to the project goal. I bring both stakeholders, or the sponsor who owns the decision, to agree on criteria such as value, risk and deadline, use MoSCoW or value versus effort to decide, and record the decision and its rationale in the backlog so it is not reopened every week.

interview.q: Which elicitation techniques do you know, and when do you use each?
interview.a: Document analysis to prepare and learn the rules, interviews for depth and individual concerns, observation to see the real work and workarounds, workshops to converge and decide with several stakeholders, surveys to reach many users, and prototypes to get concrete feedback. I combine them: read, interview, observe, then validate in a workshop, and I always send a written summary.

interview.q: How do you write a good non-functional requirement?
interview.a: I make it measurable with a metric, a target and a context, for example 'the search answers in under 2 seconds for 95% of requests with 200 concurrent users'. I ask about performance, availability, security, accessibility and data retention during discovery, check feasibility and cost with the tech lead, and put cross-cutting ones in the Definition of Done and specific ones in the story's acceptance criteria.

interview.q: How do you prioritise when MoSCoW is not enough?
interview.a: I use value versus effort for a quick view, and cost of delay or WSJF when timing matters: cost of delay divided by size brings small, urgent items forward, such as a regulatory deadline. The Kano model helps make sure basic needs are covered before adding delighters. I score with the stakeholders, relatively, and record the rationale with the decision.

interview.q: How do you specify a report or a dashboard?
interview.a: I start from the decisions it supports and its audience, then define each measure with a precise calculation rule, the dimensions, filters, refresh frequency, sources and access rights, and I check the terms against the data dictionary. I validate a mock-up with real figures and a worked example per measure, which then become the test cases for UAT.

interview.q: What is the difference between severity and priority of a defect? Give an example.
interview.a: Severity is the impact on the business or the system, usually blocking, major or minor; priority is how urgently we fix it, decided in triage with the product owner. They are independent: a typo in the company name on the login page is minor but high priority because every customer sees it; a wrong total in a yearly report used in December can be major but wait until the next release if we are in March.

interview.q: UAT ends tomorrow and some defects are still open. How do you prepare the go / no-go decision?
interview.a: I compare the figures with the exit criteria agreed before the campaign: share of test cases run and passed, open defects by severity, and for each remaining one the impact, the workaround and the fix date. I check that fixed defects were retested by the business. I present the facts and a recommendation, the sponsor decides, and the result goes into the PV de recette, with the open defects listed as reservations if we go.

interview.q: Do agile teams still need a functional specification (SFD)?
interview.a: Not a large document written before the work starts, but often a light, living specification per feature: the business rules with identifiers, the screens and fields, the error cases and the data, linked to the stories. It is needed when the rules are complex or regulated, when a supplier works under a fixed-price contract, when an interface is agreed with another team, and for support and audits after go-live. I choose the level of detail by risk and audience.
